lessons.title: From production targets to a plan
lessons.html:
What operational planning is

Operational planning turns the farm's goals into a schedule of who does what, when and with which resources. Strategic plans say 'produce 40 tonnes of tilapia a year'. Operational plans say which units are stocked in which week, how much feed is needed each month and who harvests on which day.

Start with the target and work backwards

  1. Set the output target: tonnes per year, and how it must be spread across months to supply buyers.
  2. Work out harvests needed: for example, 40 tonnes at 500 g per fish means 80 000 fish harvested.
  3. Allow for survival: if survival from stocking to harvest is 80%, you must stock 100 000 fingerlings.
  4. Allow for growth time: the number of weeks from stocking to market size, which is longer in winter for warm-water species.
  5. Fit the batches to unit capacity: how much biomass each pond or tank can carry at the planned density.

Staggered production

Stocking all units at once gives one big harvest and long periods with no income and idle staff. Staggered stocking, for example a new batch every month or every quarter, smooths cash flow, workload and supply to buyers. It also lets you rest and clean units between batches.

Seasonality in South Africa

Warm-water species grow fast in summer and very slowly in winter in most inland areas, unless water is heated. Trout farming in cold areas faces the opposite problem in hot summers. Plan stocking so that the fastest growth phase falls in the best season, and avoid stressful work such as grading in the hottest weeks.

Resources the plan must cover

  • Fingerling supply: order dates and supplier lead times.
  • Feed by type and size per month.
  • Labour per week, including harvest peaks.
  • Equipment and maintenance windows.
  • Cash flow.

lessons.title: Scheduling, monitoring and adjusting
lessons.html:
Making the plan usable

A plan only works if the team can see it and use it. Break it down into calendars and checklists.

Planning tools

  • Production calendar: a chart showing each unit across the weeks of the year, with stocking, grading, sampling and harvest dates.
  • Weekly work plan: tasks per day per person.
  • Feed plan: forecast feed per unit per week, based on biomass and feeding rate tables.
  • Maintenance schedule: planned servicing fitted into gaps between batches.

Setting objectives

Objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART). For example: 'Harvest 3 000 kg of tilapia from Ponds 4 and 5 in the week of 10 March, with survival above the budgeted figure.'

Monitoring

Each week compare actual results with the plan:

IndicatorPlanActualAction
Average weight Pond 4380 g340 gCheck feeding and water; delay harvest?
Mortalities this weekUnder 0.5%1.2%Health check, call vet

The figures above are examples only; set your own targets from your records.

Contingency planning

Ask 'what if' questions and prepare responses: power failure, feed delivery delay, disease outbreak, drought reducing water supply, a key worker leaving, a buyer cancelling. For each, decide early warning signs, the immediate response and who is responsible.

Adjusting the plan

Plans change. If growth is slower than expected, harvest dates move, feed orders change and buyers must be told. Update the plan, communicate the changes to the team and record why they were made, so next year's plan is more accurate.

Key points

  • Work backwards from the output target, allowing for survival and growth time.
  • Stagger stocking to smooth cash flow, workload and supply.
  • Plan around seasonal growth in South African conditions.
  • Monitor actual results against the plan weekly.
  • Prepare contingency plans and update the plan when conditions change.
